content: Language disorders in children are characterized by difficulties in either expressing their thoughts and messages to others (expressive language disorder) or understanding the messages conveyed by others (receptive language disorder). Some children may only have expressive language disorder, while others may experience a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, which involves symptoms of both conditions. Despite these challenges, children with language disorders are typically able to produce sounds, and their speech can often be understood. Symptoms of Language Disorders A child with a language disorder may exhibit one or more of the following symptoms, which can range from mild to severe: Receptive Language Disorder Symptoms: Children with receptive language disorders struggle to understand language. They may: Have difficulty comprehending what others are saying. Struggle to follow spoken directions. Experience challenges in organizing their thoughts. Expressive Language Disorder Symptoms: Children with expressive language disorders have trouble using language to express their thoughts or needs. They may: Struggle to construct sentences, often producing simple or short sentences with incorrect word order. Have difficulty finding the right words during conversations, frequently using placeholder words like um. Possess a vocabulary that is below the expected level for their age. Omit words from sentences when speaking. Repeat certain phrases or echo parts of questions. Use verb tenses (past, present, future) incorrectly. Due to these language difficulties, children may face challenges in social settings. In some cases, language disorders can contribute to severe behavioral problems. Causes of Language Disorders Language development typically begins at birth and requires the ability to hear, see, understand, and remember, as well as the physical ability to produce speech. However, up to 1 in 20 children may exhibit symptoms of a language disorder. When the cause is unknown, the condition is referred to as a developmental language disorder. Receptive language problems often emerge before the age of 4. Mixed language disorders may result from brain injuries, which can sometimes be misdiagnosed as developmental disorders. Language disorders can also occur in children with other developmental issues, autism spectrum disorders, hearing loss, or learning disabilities. Damage to the central nervous system, known as aphasia, can also lead to language disorders. Importantly, language disorders are rarely caused by a lack of intelligence. Language disorders differ from delayed language development. In delayed language, the child develops speech and language in the same way as other children but at a slower pace. In contrast, language disorders involve abnormal development of speech and language, with some skills developing while others do not, or with an atypical developmental pattern. When to Seek Medical Care Parents concerned about their child’s speech or language development should consult their primary care provider and inquire about a referral to a speech and language therapist. Children diagnosed with language disorders may also need evaluation by a neurologist or developmental specialist to determine if the underlying cause can be treated. Parents should contact their child’s healthcare provider if they observe the following signs of difficulty understanding language: At 15 months: The child does not look at or point to 5–10 people or objects when named by a parent or caregiver. At 18 months: The child does not follow simple spoken directions, such as get your coat. At 24 months: The child cannot point to a picture or body part when named. At 30 months: The child does not respond to questions by nodding, shaking their head, or speaking. At 36 months: The child does not follow two-step directions or understand action words. Additionally, parents should seek help if their child shows signs of difficulty using or expressing language: At 15 months: The child is not using three words. At 18 months: The child is not saying Mama, Dada, or other
